sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Decompose \(\frac{5x-1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\) into partial fractions.
questions.target: Partial fraction decomposition: distinct linear factors

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int\frac{3x+5}{x^2+x-2}\,dx\) using partial fractions (note \(x^2+x-2=(x+2)(x-1)\)).
questions.target: Partial fraction decomposition: distinct linear factors

questions.q: Decompose \(\frac{x+7}{x^2-x-6}\) into partial fractions (note \(x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)\)).
questions.target: Partial fraction decomposition: distinct linear factors

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int\frac{2x+3}{(x-1)^2}\,dx\) using the decomposition found above.
questions.target: Partial fractions with a repeated linear factor
questions.answer: \(\int\left(\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{5}{(x-1)^2}\right)dx=2\ln|x-1|-\frac{5}{x-1}+C\).
questions.explanation: \(\int\left(\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{5}{(x-1)^2}\right)dx=2\ln|x-1|-\frac{5}{x-1}+C\).

questions.q: Set up (but do not solve for constants) the partial fraction decomposition of \(\frac{3x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+4)}\).
questions.target: Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor
questions.answer: Since \(x^2+4\) is irreducible over the reals, the decomposition has the form \(\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}\).
questions.explanation: Since \(x^2+4\) is irreducible over the reals, the decomposition has the form \(\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}\).

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx\), or show it diverges.
questions.target: Improper integrals: infinite limits
questions.answer: \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=\lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^b=\lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left(-\frac{1}{b}+1\right)=0+1=1\). Converges to \(1\).
questions.explanation: \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=\lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^b=\lim_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left(-\frac{1}{b}+1\right)=0+1=1\). Converges to \(1\).

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_0^1\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx\), or show it diverges (note the integrand is undefined at \(x=0\)).
questions.target: Improper integrals: discontinuous integrands
questions.answer: \(\int_0^1x^{-1/2}\,dx=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_a^1=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}(2-2\sqrt{a})=2-0=2\). Converges to \(2\).
questions.explanation: \(\int_0^1x^{-1/2}\,dx=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_a^1=\lim_{a\rightarrow0^+}(2-2\sqrt{a})=2-0=2\). Converges to \(2\).

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_0^2\frac{1}{(x-2)^2}\,dx\), or show it diverges (the integrand is undefined at \(x=2\)).
questions.target: Improper integrals: discontinuous integrands
questions.answer: \(\int_0^2(x-2)^{-2}\,dx=\lim_{b\rightarrow2^-}\left[-\frac{1}{x-2}\right]_0^b=\lim_{b\rightarrow2^-}\left(-\frac{1}{b-2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\infty\). Diverges.
questions.explanation: \(\int_0^2(x-2)^{-2}\,dx=\lim_{b\rightarrow2^-}\left[-\frac{1}{x-2}\right]_0^b=\lim_{b\rightarrow2^-}\left(-\frac{1}{b-2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\infty\). Diverges.

questions.q: State the p-test for \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\), and use it to determine convergence for \(p=3\) and \(p=0.5\).
questions.target: The p-test for improper integrals
questions.answer: \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\) converges if \(p>1\) and diverges if \(p\leq1\). For \(p=3>1\): converges. For \(p=0.5\leq1\): diverges.
questions.explanation: \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\) converges if \(p>1\) and diverges if \(p\leq1\). For \(p=3>1\): converges. For \(p=0.5\leq1\): diverges.

questions.q: State the analogous p-test for \(\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\) (a discontinuity at \(x=0\)), and determine convergence for \(p=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(p=2\).
questions.target: The p-test for improper integrals
questions.answer: \(\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\) converges if \(p<1\) and diverges if \(p\geq1\) (opposite condition from the infinite-limit case). For \(p=\frac{1}{2}<1\): converges. For \(p=2\geq1\): diverges.
questions.explanation: \(\int_0^1\frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\) converges if \(p<1\) and diverges if \(p\geq1\) (opposite condition from the infinite-limit case). For \(p=\frac{1}{2}<1\): converges. For \(p=2\geq1\): diverges.

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx\) using partial fractions.
questions.target: Combining partial fractions with improper integrals
questions.answer: \(\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\). \(\int_0^{b}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[\ln\frac{x+1}{x+2}\right]_0^b=\ln\frac{b+1}{b+2}-\ln\frac{1}{2}\). As \(b\rightarrow\infty\), \(\frac{b+1}{b+2}\rightarrow1\), so the limit is \(\ln1-\ln\frac{1}{2}=\ln2\). Converges to \(\ln2\).
questions.explanation: \(\frac{1}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\). \(\int_0^{b}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[\ln\frac{x+1}{x+2}\right]_0^b=\ln\frac{b+1}{b+2}-\ln\frac{1}{2}\). As \(b\rightarrow\infty\), \(\frac{b+1}{b+2}\rightarrow1\), so the limit is \(\ln1-\ln\frac{1}{2}=\ln2\). Converges to \(\ln2\).

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int\frac{6x^2-3x-1}{x(x-1)(x+1)}\,dx\) using the decomposition above.
questions.target: Three distinct linear factors
questions.answer: \(\int\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{4}{x+1}\right)dx=\ln|x|+\ln|x-1|+4\ln|x+1|+C\).
questions.explanation: \(\int\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{4}{x+1}\right)dx=\ln|x|+\ln|x-1|+4\ln|x+1|+C\).

questions.q: The convergent improper integral \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=1\) (shown earlier) means the infinite region under \(y=\frac{1}{x^2}\) for \(x\geq1\) has FINITE area. Explain intuitively why this is possible even though the region extends forever.
questions.target: Visualizing convergence: area under the curve
questions.answer: Even though the region is infinitely long, the height \(\frac{1}{x^2}\) shrinks fast enough as \(x\rightarrow\infty\) that the accumulated area still converges to a finite total — the 'tail' contributes less and less area, summing to a bounded amount, similar to how a convergent geometric series sums to a finite value despite infinitely many terms.
questions.explanation: Even though the region is infinitely long, the height \(\frac{1}{x^2}\) shrinks fast enough as \(x\rightarrow\infty\) that the accumulated area still converges to a finite total — the 'tail' contributes less and less area, summing to a bounded amount, similar to how a convergent geometric series sums to a finite value despite infinitely many terms.

questions.q: In the partial fraction decomposition \( \dfrac{1}{(x-3)(x-5)}=\dfrac{A}{x-3}+\dfrac{B}{x-5} \), find \(A\).
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. Multiply by \((x-3)(x-5)\): \(1=A(x-5)+B(x-3)\). Set \(x=3\): \(1=A(3-5)\Rightarrow A=\dfrac{1}{3-5}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}(1+x)}\,dx\) is a classic doubly-improper integral (discontinuous at \(x=0\) AND infinite upper bound). Explain how such an integral must be split to evaluate it.
questions.target: Improper integrals with both an infinite bound and a discontinuity
questions.answer: Split at any convenient interior point, e.g. \(x=1\): \(\int_0^{\infty}=\int_0^1+\int_1^{\infty}\). Each piece is evaluated as its own limit (one with \(a\rightarrow0^+\), the other with \(b\rightarrow\infty\)), and the original integral converges only if BOTH pieces converge.
questions.explanation: Split at any convenient interior point, e.g. \(x=1\): \(\int_0^{\infty}=\int_0^1+\int_1^{\infty}\). Each piece is evaluated as its own limit (one with \(a\rightarrow0^+\), the other with \(b\rightarrow\infty\)), and the original integral converges only if BOTH pieces converge.

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to argue that \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx\) converges, without computing it exactly.
questions.target: Comparison test for improper integrals
questions.cross_lesson: 5.01 Sequences and Basic Series Convergence Tests
questions.answer: For \(x\geq1\): \(\frac{1}{x^2+1}<\frac{1}{x^2}\). Since \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx\) converges (shown earlier, \(p=2>1\)), and the given integrand is smaller and positive, \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx\) also converges by comparison.
questions.explanation: For \(x\geq1\): \(\frac{1}{x^2+1}<\frac{1}{x^2}\). Since \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx\) converges (shown earlier, \(p=2>1\)), and the given integrand is smaller and positive, \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx\) also converges by comparison.

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to argue that \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\,dx\) diverges.
questions.target: Comparison test for improper integrals
questions.cross_lesson: 5.02 Ratio, Root, and Alternating Series Tests
questions.answer: Since \(-1\leq\sin x\leq1\), we have \(2+\sin x\geq1\), so \(\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{1}{x}\) for \(x\geq1\). Since \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,dx\) diverges, and the given integrand is at least as large, \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\,dx\) also diverges by comparison.
questions.explanation: Since \(-1\leq\sin x\leq1\), we have \(2+\sin x\geq1\), so \(\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{1}{x}\) for \(x\geq1\). Since \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}\,dx\) diverges, and the given integrand is at least as large, \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{2+\sin x}{x}\,dx\) also diverges by comparison.

questions.q: Level 3 · Advanced / AP FRQThe alternating series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^4}\) converges to sum \(S\). If the sum is approximated by the fourth partial sum \(S_4\), use the Alternating Series Error Bound to find an upper bound for the error \(|S - S_4|\).
questions.target: Combining partial fractions with improper integrals
questions.cross_lesson: 6.01 Power Series and Interval of Convergence
questions.answer: The series satisfies the hypotheses of the AST: \(a_n = \frac{1}{n^4}\) is positive, strictly decreasing, and \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{1}{n^4} = 0\). By the Alternating Series Error Bound: \(|S - S_4| \leq a_5 = \frac{1}{5^4} = \frac{1}{625} = \mathbf{0.0016}.\) The approximation error is guaranteed to be less than or equal to 0.0016.
questions.explanation: The series satisfies the hypotheses of the AST: \(a_n = \frac{1}{n^4}\) is positive, strictly decreasing, and \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{1}{n^4} = 0\). By the Alternating Series Error Bound: \(|S - S_4| \leq a_5 = \frac{1}{5^4} = \frac{1}{625} = \mathbf{0.0016}.\) The approximation error is guaranteed to be less than or equal to 0.0016.

questions.q: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int x e^{8x}\,dx \) using integration by parts.
questions.answer: **Answer:** D. By parts with \(u=x,\ dv=e^{8x}dx\): \(v=\tfrac18e^{8x}\). \(\int xe^{8x}dx=\dfrac{x}{8}e^{8x}-\dfrac18\int e^{8x}dx=\dfrac{8x-1}{64}e^{8x}+C.\)
questions.explanation: By parts with \(u=x,\ dv=e^{8x}dx\): \(v=\tfrac18e^{8x}\). \(\int xe^{8x}dx=\dfrac{x}{8}e^{8x}-\dfrac18\int e^{8x}dx=\dfrac{8x-1}{64}e^{8x}+C.\)

questions.q: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int x\sin(5x)\,dx \) using integration by parts.
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. \(u=x,\ dv=\sin(5x)dx\Rightarrow v=-\tfrac15\cos(5x)\). \(\int x\sin(5x)dx=-\dfrac{x}{5}\cos(5x)+\dfrac15\int\cos(5x)dx=-\dfrac{x}{5}\cos(5x)+\dfrac1{25}\sin(5x)+C.\)
questions.explanation: \(u=x,\ dv=\sin(5x)dx\Rightarrow v=-\tfrac15\cos(5x)\). \(\int x\sin(5x)dx=-\dfrac{x}{5}\cos(5x)+\dfrac15\int\cos(5x)dx=-\dfrac{x}{5}\cos(5x)+\dfrac1{25}\sin(5x)+C.\)

questions.q: Use a direct comparison to determine whether \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\,dx\) converges or diverges.
questions.target: Partial fraction decomposition: distinct linear factors
choices: Diverges only because \(a=4\) happens to be even.
Diverges, since \(\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{3}{x}\) for \(x\geq1\), and \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x}\,dx\) diverges since \(p=1\leq1\).
Converges, since \(\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\leq\frac{5}{x}\) for \(x\geq1\), and \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{5}{x}\,dx\) converges since \(p=1>1\).
Cannot be determined by comparison, since \(\sin x\) oscillates.
questions.answer: Since \(-1\leq\sin x\leq1\): Diverges, since \(\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{3}{x}\) for \(x\geq1\), and \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x}\,dx\) diverges since \(p=1\leq1\).
questions.explanation: Since \(-1\leq\sin x\leq1\): Diverges, since \(\frac{4+\sin x}{x}\geq\frac{3}{x}\) for \(x\geq1\), and \(\int_1^{\infty}\frac{3}{x}\,dx\) diverges since \(p=1\leq1\).

questions.q: Evaluate \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)}\) using partial fractions (telescoping).
questions.target: Partial fractions with a repeated linear factor
questions.answer: \(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}=\frac{1}{1}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\). Telescoping leaves \(\frac{1}{1}\left(1+\frac{1}{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{1}\right)=1.\)
questions.explanation: \(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}=\frac{1}{1}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\). Telescoping leaves \(\frac{1}{1}\left(1+\frac{1}{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{1}\right)=1.\)

questions.q: Use the comparison test to determine whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{2}+6}\) converges.
questions.target: Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor
questions.answer: Since \(01\)), the given series converges by the comparison test.
questions.explanation: Since \(01\)), the given series converges by the comparison test.

questions.q: Consider the infinite series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^p}{5^n}\). The series converges if and only if the parameter \(p\) satisfies which of the following conditions? Use the Ratio Test to determine the interval of convergence.
questions.target: Improper integrals: infinite limits
questions.answer: We apply the Ratio Test. Let \(a_n = \frac{n^p}{5^n}\). Then \(a_{n+1} = \frac{(n+1)^p}{5^{n+1}}\). We compute the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms: \(L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{(n+1)^p}{5^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{5^n}{n^p} \right|\) \(L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{1}{5} \left( \frac{n+1}{n} \right)^p \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{1}{5} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^p \right|\) As \(n \rightarrow \infty\), \(\frac{1}{n} \rightarrow 0\), so \(\left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^p \rightarrow 1^p = 1\) for any real \(p\). Thus, \(L = \frac{1}{5} \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{5}\) . According to the Ratio Test, the series converges if \(L < 1\). Since \(L = \frac{1}{5} < 1\) for all real values of \(p\), the series converges for all real values of \(p\).
questions.explanation: We apply the Ratio Test. Let \(a_n = \frac{n^p}{5^n}\). Then \(a_{n+1} = \frac{(n+1)^p}{5^{n+1}}\). We compute the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms: \(L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{(n+1)^p}{5^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{5^n}{n^p} \right|\) \(L = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{1}{5} \left( \frac{n+1}{n} \right)^p \right| = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \left| \frac{1}{5} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^p \right|\) As \(n \rightarrow \infty\), \(\frac{1}{n} \rightarrow 0\), so \(\left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^p \rightarrow 1^p = 1\) for any real \(p\). Thus, \(L = \frac{1}{5} \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{5}\) . According to the Ratio Test, the series converges if \(L < 1\). Since \(L = \frac{1}{5} < 1\) for all real values of \(p\), the series converges for all real values of \(p\).

questions.q: For \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^{2}}{2^{n}}\), apply the ratio test and determine convergence.
questions.target: Improper integrals: discontinuous integrands
questions.answer: \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}<1\). Ratio test: converges regardless of the fixed power 2.
questions.explanation: \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}<1\). Ratio test: converges regardless of the fixed power 2.

questions.q: Apply the ratio test to \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{6^{n}}{n!}\). What is \(L=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|\)?
questions.target: The p-test for improper integrals
questions.answer: \(\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\frac{6}{n+1}\rightarrow0\) as \(n\rightarrow\infty\). Since \(L=0<1\), the series converges (for every \(x\)).
questions.explanation: \(\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\frac{6}{n+1}\rightarrow0\) as \(n\rightarrow\infty\). Since \(L=0<1\), the series converges (for every \(x\)).

questions.q: Determine whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{n^{n}}\) converges using the ratio test. (variant 1)
questions.target: Combining partial fractions with improper integrals
questions.answer: \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{n^n}{(n+1)^n}=\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n\rightarrow\frac{1}{e}<1\). Ratio test: converges.
questions.explanation: \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{n^n}{(n+1)^n}=\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n\rightarrow\frac{1}{e}<1\). Ratio test: converges.

questions.q: Repeated linear factor in partial fractions: \(\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{(x-1)^2}\). Decompose \(\frac{x}{(x-1)^2}\):
questions.target: Comparison test for improper integrals
questions.answer: Applying Techniques of Integration principles, \(x=(x-1)+1\Rightarrow A=1,B=1\). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}\).

questions.q: Considering the partial fraction decomposition \( \dfrac{1}{(x-0)(x-4)}=\dfrac{A}{x-0}+\dfrac{B}{x-4} \), find \(A\).
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. Multiply by \((x-0)(x-4)\): \(1=A(x-4)+B(x-0)\). Set \(x=0\): \(1=A(0-4)\Rightarrow A=\dfrac{1}{0-4}=\dfrac{1}{4}\).

questions.q: Consider the infinite series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\). If the terms of the series are given by \(a_n = \frac{3n+1}{2n+5}\), which of the following statements about the convergence of the series is true based on the limit of the terms?
questions.target: Partial fractions with a repeated linear factor
choices: The series diverges because \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n\) does not exist.
questions.answer: To determine the convergence or divergence of an infinite series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\), we can first examine the limit of its terms, \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n\). If this limit is not equal to zero, then the series diverges by the Test for Divergence. For the given series, the terms are \(a_n = \frac{3n+1}{2n+5}\). We evaluate the limit as \(n \rightarrow \infty\): \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{3n+1}{2n+5}\) To evaluate this limit, we can divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of \(n\) in the denominator, which is \(n\): \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\frac{3n}{n}+\frac{1}{n}}{\frac{2n}{n}+\frac{5}{n}} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{3+\frac{1}{n}}{2+\frac{5}{n}}\) As \(n \rightarrow \infty\), \(\frac{1}{n} \rightarrow 0\) and \(\frac{5}{n} \rightarrow 0\). Therefore, the limit becomes: \(\frac{3+0}{2+0} = \frac{3}{2}\) Since \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n = \frac{3}{2}\), and \(\frac{3}{2} eq 0\), the series diverges by the Test for Divergence. Therefore, choice B is correct.
questions.explanation: To determine the convergence or divergence of an infinite series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\), we can first examine the limit of its terms, \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n\). If this limit is not equal to zero, then the series diverges by the Test for Divergence. For the given series, the terms are \(a_n = \frac{3n+1}{2n+5}\). We evaluate the limit as \(n \rightarrow \infty\): \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{3n+1}{2n+5}\) To evaluate this limit, we can divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of \(n\) in the denominator, which is \(n\): \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\frac{3n}{n}+\frac{1}{n}}{\frac{2n}{n}+\frac{5}{n}} = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{3+\frac{1}{n}}{2+\frac{5}{n}}\) As \(n \rightarrow \infty\), \(\frac{1}{n} \rightarrow 0\) and \(\frac{5}{n} \rightarrow 0\). Therefore, the limit becomes: \(\frac{3+0}{2+0} = \frac{3}{2}\) Since \(\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n = \frac{3}{2}\), and \(\frac{3}{2} eq 0\), the series diverges by the Test for Divergence. Therefore, choice B is correct.

questions.q: Consider the infinite series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^p}{4^n}\). For what values of \(p\) does the series converge?
questions.target: Partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor
questions.answer: We will use the Ratio Test to determine the convergence of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^p}{4^n}\). Let \(a_n = \frac{n^p}{4^n}\). Then \(a_{n+1} = \frac{(n+1)^p}{4^{n+1}}\). The ratio of consecutive terms is: \(\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \left| \frac{(n+1)^p / 4^{n+1}}{n^p / 4^n} \right| = \left| \frac{(n+1)^p}{n^p} \cdot \frac{4^n}{4^{n+1}} \right| = \left| \left( \frac{n+1}{n} \right)^p \cdot \frac{1}{4} \right| = \left| \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^p \cdot \frac{1}{4} \right|\) Now, we take the limit as \(n \rightarrow \infty\): \(L = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^p \cdot \frac{1}{4}\) Since \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right) = 1\), we have: \(L = 1^p \cdot \frac{1}{4} = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{4}\) According to the Ratio Test, if \(L < 1\), the series converges. In this case, \(L = \frac{1}{4}\), which is indeed less than 1. The limit \(L\) is independent of the value of \(p\). Therefore, the series converges for all real values of \(p\).

questions.q: Determine the numerical value of \( \displaystyle\int x e^{4x}\,dx \) using integration by parts.
questions.answer: **Answer:** D. By parts with \(u=x,\ dv=e^{4x}dx\): \(v=\tfrac14e^{4x}\). \(\int xe^{4x}dx=\dfrac{x}{4}e^{4x}-\dfrac14\int e^{4x}dx=\dfrac{4x-1}{16}e^{4x}+C.\)

questions.q: Consider the polar curve given by the equation \(r = 3 - 2\sin(\theta)\). A point \(P\) on this curve has polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\). If the Cartesian coordinates of \(P\) are \((x, y)\), and \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), find the value of \(x\).
questions.target: Improper integrals: discontinuous integrands
questions.answer: The relationship between polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) and Cartesian coordinates \((x, y)\) is given by \(x = r\cos(\theta)\) and \(y = r\sin(\theta)\). We are given the polar equation \(r = 3 - 2\sin(\theta)\) and that \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\). First, we find the value of \(r\) at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(r = 3 - 2\sin(\frac{\pi}{2}) = 3 - 2(1) = 1\). Now we can find the Cartesian coordinate \(x\) using \(x = r\cos(\theta)\): \(x = 1 \cdot \cos(\frac{\pi}{2}) = 1 \cdot 0 = 0\). Therefore, the value of \(x\) is 0.

questions.q: Consider the infinite sequence defined by \(a_n = \frac{3n^2 + 2n - 1}{n^2 + 5}\). To determine if this sequence converges, we examine its limit as \(n \rightarrow \infty\). Which of the following statements is true about the limit of \(a_n\)?
questions.target: The p-test for improper integrals
questions.answer: To find the limit of the sequence \(a_n = \frac{3n^2 + 2n - 1}{n^2 + 5}\) as \(n \rightarrow \infty\), we can divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of \(n\) in the denominator, which is \(n^2\). \(x\) As \(n \rightarrow \infty\), the terms \(\frac{2}{n}\), \(\frac{1}{n^2}\), and \(\frac{5}{n^2}\) all approach 0. \(= \frac{3 + 0 - 0}{1 + 0} = \frac{3}{1} = 3\) Therefore, the sequence converges to 3.

questions.q: The polar curve is given by the equation \(r = 4 \cos(\theta)\). What is the equivalent Cartesian equation for this curve?
questions.target: Combining partial fractions with improper integrals
questions.answer: We know the relationships between polar and Cartesian coordinates: \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2\), \(x = r \cos(\theta)\), and \(y = r \sin(\theta)\). The given polar equation is \(r = 4 \cos(\theta)\). To convert this to a Cartesian equation, we can multiply both sides by \(r\) to get \(r^2 = 4r \cos(\theta)\). Substituting the Cartesian equivalents, we have \(x^2 + y^2 = 4x\).

questions.answer: The given series is the p-series, \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^p}\). This series is a fundamental example in the study of convergence. The p-series test states that the p-series converges if and only if \(p > 1\). Therefore, the series converges for \(p > 1\).
